source.version: arXiv v1 of 2026-04-13 (arXiv:2604.11019v1 [cs.HC], per the margin stamp on PDF p. 1); full PDF read, numbers checked on PDF pp. 13-18
source.title_on_document: Brief2Design: A Multi-phased, Compositional Approach to Prompt-based Graphic Design

supplement.where: Appendix A, PDF pp. 26-30; Appendix B, PDF pp. 30-34, including Tables 2-5.
supplement.holds: Appendix A contains the system prompts for all modules. Appendix B contains the task briefs and participant output gallery. These appendices do not supply additional inferential-result tables or standard errors.

paper_design_summary: Six CyberAgent designers took part in remote formative interviews about their workflows (p. 5, Sec. 3.1), followed by a separate 12-designer evaluation (p. 13, Sec. 6.1; p. 23, Sec. 8.6.1). Evaluation participants were assigned four graphic-design briefs, two with Brief2Design and two with a conversational baseline using the same models; task order was fixed, system order was counterbalanced within each freedom condition, and some tasks were incomplete (pp. 13-16, Secs. 6.2-7.1). The authors measured within-participant image and prompt diversity separately for all logged generated final images and the target set of two submitted images, plus generated-image counts, completion, time, and self-reported creativity support (pp. 15-18, Secs. 6.4-7.4).

studies.label: User evaluation: within-subjects comparison of Brief2Design and a conversational baseline (counterbalanced system order, randomization not stated)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the two systems (Brief2Design vs conversational baseline) within each task condition; every participant used both systems, two tasks each, with a fixed task order
assignment.quote: The order of the four tasks was fixed, while the order of the systems was counterbalanced within each task condition.
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration statement in the full document, including appendices (PDF pp. 1-34); evaluation methods and results: pp. 13-19, Secs. 6-7.

arms.name: Brief2Design
arms.description: Structured three-step tool: requirement extraction and recommendation, element-level card exploration, then integration of selected elements into one design via text-to-image generation

arms.name: Baseline
arms.description: Conversational AI interface similar to ChatGPT (ReAct agent with the image model as a tool), same LLM and image model as Brief2Design

participants.exclusions: Image and prompt diversity analyses retained only paired tasks with two submitted images, yielding 7 paired participants for low-freedom tasks and 8 for high-freedom tasks (PDF p. 18, Sec. 7.3). P4's low-freedom Baseline observation was omitted from completion-time analysis because images were submitted with an experimenter's help after task completion following a misunderstanding of the experiment system (PDF p. 16, Sec. 7.1). The overall 12-person study count does not mean that every participant contributed to each diversity comparison; generated-image counts were analyzed for the full sample (PDF p. 13, Sec. 6.1; pp. 16-17, Sec. 7.2).
participants.who: 12 designers at the authors' company (7 women, 5 men; mean age 27.1; design experience 5 months to 20 years, mean 4.2 years), taking part as regular work. Every participant used both systems. The diversity analysis kept only tasks where both images were submitted: 7 paired data points (low-freedom) and 8 (high-freedom).
participants.quote: We recruited 12 designers (P1-12; 7 women and 5 men, age: M = 27.1, SD = 6.8) from our company.
participants.locator: p. 13, Sec. 6.1; p. 18, Sec. 7.3 (7 and 8 data points)

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI GPT-4o (LLM steps) and OpenAI gpt-image-1 (image generation), used in both systems (p. 13, Sec. 5.5; p. 13, Sec. 6.2)
ai_tool.how_used: Participants generated design images one at a time either through Brief2Design's requirement and element cards or through free chat with the conversational baseline, with a target of submitting two sufficiently different design proposals per task; some tasks were incomplete (PDF pp. 13-16, Secs. 6.2-7.1).

task.description: Create two sufficiently different design proposals (images) for a client brief: four briefs (cosmetics signage ad, gym direct mail, music festival SNS post, restaurant recruitment poster), two low-freedom and two high-freedom
task.duration: 15 minutes per task; about 120 minutes in total including practice (pp. 13-15, Secs. 6.3-6.4)

outcomes.name: Image diversity of submitted images (average pairwise 1 - cosine of DreamSim embeddings within a participant's set for one task)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Average pairwise dissimilarity (1 minus cosine similarity) of DreamSim image embeddings within each participant's submitted-image set for a task. Paired tests retain tasks with two submitted images under both systems: 7 paired participants in low freedom and 8 in high freedom. Figure 8 shows means graphically without numerical mean labels (PDF p. 15, Sec. 6.5; pp. 17-18, Fig. 8 and Sec. 7.3).

contrasts.reported: Submitted images, low-freedom tasks: t(6) = 1.91, p = .105; 7 paired data points.
Submitted images, high-freedom tasks: t(7) = .820, p = .439; 8 paired data points.

outcomes.name: Image diversity of all generated images (average pairwise 1 - cosine of DreamSim embeddings within a participant's set for one task)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Average pairwise dissimilarity (1 minus cosine similarity) of DreamSim embeddings within each participant's set of all logged generated final images for a task. Element-level preview images were not logged. Despite using all generated final images, paired analyses retain only tasks with two submitted images under both systems: 7 paired participants in low freedom and 8 in high freedom. Means appear graphically without numerical labels in Figure 8 (PDF p. 15, Sec. 6.5; pp. 17-18, Fig. 8 and Sec. 7.3).

contrasts.reported: Generated images, low-freedom tasks: t(6) = .824, p = .441; 7 paired data points.
Generated images, high-freedom tasks: t(7) = −1.16, p = .283; 8 paired data points.

outcomes.name: Prompt diversity (average pairwise 1 - cosine of OpenAI text-embedding-3-large embeddings of the prompts within a participant's set for one task)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Average pairwise dissimilarity (1 minus cosine similarity) of text-embedding-3-large embeddings within each participant's task-specific prompt set. Analyzed separately for prompts corresponding to all logged generated final images and to submitted images; paired analyses retain tasks with two submitted images under both systems, with 7 paired participants in low freedom and 8 in high freedom. This measures within-person variety. Figure 9 shows means graphically without numerical mean labels (PDF p. 15, Sec. 6.5; pp. 17-18, Fig. 9 and Sec. 7.3).

contrasts.reported: Prompts for generated images, low-freedom tasks: t(6) = 3.86, p = .008; 7 paired data points; Brief2Design higher.
Prompts for generated images, high-freedom tasks: t(7) = 1.69, p = .134; 8 paired data points.
Prompts for submitted images, low-freedom tasks: t(6) = 2.00, p = .093; 7 paired data points; described as marginally significant by the authors.
Prompts for submitted images, high-freedom tasks: t(7) = 2.45, p = .044; 8 paired data points; Brief2Design higher.

outcomes.name: Number of generated final design images
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of final design images generated per participant-task from system logs, compared with paired t-tests within each freedom condition for the 12-person study sample. Element-level preview images were not logged (PDF p. 13, Sec. 6.1; p. 15, Sec. 6.5; pp. 16-17, Sec. 7.2).

contrasts.reported: Low-freedom tasks, Brief2Design M = 4.2 (SD = 1.4) vs Baseline M = 4.8 (SD = 2.1); paired t(11) = −1.07, p = .309; 12-person paired sample.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 16, Sec. 7.2; p. 13, Sec. 6.1 (study sample).

contrasts.reported: High-freedom tasks, Brief2Design M = 3.8 (SD = 0.9) vs Baseline M = 5.4 (SD = 1.2); paired t(11) = −4.71, p = .001; 12-person paired sample.
contrasts.locator: PDF pp. 16-17, Sec. 7.2; p. 13, Sec. 6.1 (study sample).

studies.label: Formative study: remote qualitative interviews with professional designers

assignment.what_was_assigned: No assigned AI-assistance contrast. Designers were interviewed about their existing workflows and challenges; this qualitative study did not score creative outputs.
assignment.quote: The study was conducted as a 60-minute semi-structured interview via online conferencing.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 5, Secs. 3 and 3.1. Assignment structure is not applicable to these interviews.
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration statement in the full document, including appendices (PDF pp. 1-34); interview procedure: p. 5, Sec. 3.1.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions stated. The formative interview sample and the user-evaluation sample were separate participant groups (PDF p. 23, Sec. 8.6.1).
participants.who: Six designers (D1-D6) from CyberAgent, the authors' company, with professional design experience ranging from 10 to 28 years (PDF p. 5, Sec. 3.1).
participants.quote: We recruited six designers (D1-6; 4 men and 2 women, age: 𝑀= 40.3, 𝑆𝐷= 5.5) from our company.
participants.locator: PDF p. 5, Sec. 3.1; p. 23, Sec. 8.6.1 (separate participant groups).

ai_tool.how_used: No AI tool was assigned for an experimental task; interviews concerned existing design practice (PDF p. 5, Sec. 3.1).

task.description: Semi-structured interviews about receiving design requests, defining requirements, generating ideas and variations, determining visual elements, and feedback and revision. Transcripts and materials were analyzed qualitatively for common behavioral patterns and challenges; no scored creativity or diversity outcome (PDF p. 5, Secs. 3-3.1).

company_involvement.description: Both authors are affiliated with CyberAgent. Designers in both studies were recruited from their company and participated as part of their regular work, without additional compensation. The company internal ethics review board approved both studies.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1, author affiliations; p. 5, Sec. 3.1; p. 13, Sec. 6.1.

eligibility.reason: The user evaluation is a counterbalanced within-subject experiment with randomization not stated; task order was fixed and system order counterbalanced (PDF p. 14, Sec. 6.3). Its 12 designers are below the 50-person threshold (p. 13, Sec. 6.1), and diversity tests use only 7 and 8 paired participants in the low- and high-freedom conditions (p. 18, Sec. 7.3). Both arms use generative AI with the same models, constituting an ai_design contrast (p. 13, Secs. 5.5-6.2). Image and prompt distances are scored on task outputs, but compare each participant's own outputs and therefore measure flexibility, not diversity across people (p. 15, Sec. 6.5; p. 18, Sec. 7.3). The separate formative interview study has six designers, no assigned AI-assistance contrast, and no scored creative-output outcome; its participants are not combined with the evaluation sample (p. 5, Secs. 3-3.1; p. 23, Sec. 8.6.1). Core exclusion is retained, with context_class=none.

one_line_finding: In the 12-designer evaluation, submitted-image diversity showed no statistically significant difference between Brief2Design and Baseline (low freedom: 7 paired participants, t(6) = 1.91, p = .105; high freedom: 8 paired participants, t(7) = .820, p = .439), while prompt diversity was significantly higher only for generated low-freedom prompts (t(6) = 3.86, p = .008) and submitted high-freedom prompts (t(7) = 2.45, p = .044), with no statistically significant difference in the other two prompt comparisons (p. 13, Sec. 6.1; pp. 17-18, Figs. 8-9 and Sec. 7.3).

Listed in the screening report as a randomized-style experiment below 50 participants.

The separate formative interview study has six designers, no assigned AI-assistance contrast, and no scored creative-output outcome; its participants are not combined with the evaluation sample (p. 5, Secs. 3-3.1; p. 23, Sec. 8.6.1). Core exclusion is retained, with context_class=none.

applied.old: Among 12 company designers, Brief2Design did not change the image diversity of submitted designs relative to a conversational baseline (low-freedom t(6) = 1.91, p = .105; high-freedom t(7) = .820, p = .439) but raised prompt diversity (e.g., submitted high-freedom t(7) = 2.45, p = .044) (p. 18, Sec. 7.3; p. 17, Figs. 8-9).
applied.new: In the 12-designer evaluation, submitted-image diversity showed no statistically significant difference between Brief2Design and Baseline (low freedom: 7 paired participants, t(6) = 1.91, p = .105; high freedom: 8 paired participants, t(7) = .820, p = .439), while prompt diversity was significantly higher only for generated low-freedom prompts (t(6) = 3.86, p = .008) and submitted high-freedom prompts (t(7) = 2.45, p = .044), with no statistically significant difference in the other two prompt comparisons (p. 13, Sec. 6.1; pp. 17-18, Figs. 8-9 and Sec. 7.3).
